questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go somewhere far away, where I also hadn't already been. I've always wanted to live in one of Asia's megacities, so Seoul seemed perfect. The Korean nature also attracted me, as I wanted to do some hiking curing my exchange.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I got ill halfway through.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Easy - Korea is also incredibly efficient.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: My host univeristy sent out several informative emails, and we got assigned local 'buddies'.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Easy. I used enkorstay, but then you'll have to pay extra fees. There's also staykorea and goshipages. You can avoid paying extra fees, if you contact the goshiwon directly. If you find an area where you'd like to stay, you can also have a look on naver maps, and find something on there.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Living off campus is oftentimes cheaper, and also nicer. It is also a great opportunity to get outside of the university bubble, if you find somewhere a bit further away. I stayed in Hyehwa, and loved the area!

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I stayed at Glade143. It's a bit on the expensive side, but the acommodation is super nice, clean, and decently big - each room also has windows with a view of the street, and the location is superb.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Stressful. Many emails. A lot of information, and many deadlines, but fairly easy. Read all of the emails carefully, and team up with other students going to the same uni.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It's all a blur. Course registration was super stressful - in the middle of the night - but plan it out carefully, and you will probably get most of the courses that you want.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: They respond to emails super fast!

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Pretty successful. I got two or three of the courses that I wanted in the first round, but two of those actually ended up being the courses that i disliked the most. My favourite course was the one that I added last, only because it was available and fit into my schedule.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Sign up for the courses that seem intimdating and and maybe a bit too hard - the ones that are mostly aimed towards local students. Those are more intersting and engaging, and the academic level usually isn't that high. 

Also, sign up for 6 course if you are in doubt, and drop the one you dislike the most during the add and drop period.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I only had one course that I really disliked. It was an easy course aimed towards internationals and exchange students. It was called something like "The City of Seoul: interdisciplinary insights". The professor was super sweet, but the course was not very acaddemic at all - which really disappointed me.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: A few of my courses required a lot of work and reading, but those were also the most interesting ones! You probably would have been able to pass without putting in too much work, but I liked the courses and felt motivated to doowell, even though the grads do not count.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: A lot more strict, and it's important to show respect towards your professors. All lectures are mandatory, and there is not much room to plan your own everyday life while at uni. The professors decide how and when everything should be done, and the students do not have much of a say.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Cognitive Psychology, Introduction to Korean Thought, Introduction to Political Science, City of Seoul, and Crafting Creative Prose.

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
My favourite courses were Cognitive Psychology, Korean Thought, and Political Science.
The professor teaching
Pol.sci
. is incredibly talented as a lecturer, and well known for being so - I was told by my Korean peers, that she is ranked among the top lecturers at Korea University.
Korean Thought requires more independent study, but if you are interested in philosophy and religion it's great! Professor -NAME REDACTED-  is incredibly knowledgeable and friendly, she even invited me out for a coffee after the semester was done. I LOVED Korean Thought, but I think the course is what you make of it.
Cognitive psychology was super interesting, and I really liked professor -NAME REDACTED-. The course gives a general introduction to a myriad of different theories and reasearch, even connecting them historically within the evolution of psychology as a field of study. If you find that interesting, you will probably enjoy this course.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Theres a lot of barriers to joining sports clubs as an exchange student.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Hanging out with your buddies - KUBA has A LOT of events. You can also join clubs, and a lot of clubs actually want more internationals, but information about clubs is scarce for exchange students. Ask your buddis for more info!

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Cycling/running along the streams or the hangang river, and going to cheap/free concerts at small and local venues and bars.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Travel within the country, and go hiking! Explore the bar and cafe scene in Seoul!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy - also, Seoulites are used to interacting with internationals.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Take initiative and be open! A lot of local students are eager to make international friends, but are sometimes a bit introverted or insecure about their english.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Hierarchical structures at university, and a lack of self-determination for students. The fixation with getting good grades, and presenting as a hard-working student. Going to a good university is more important than studying what you want, so a lot of students take courses that don't really interest them. Oftentimes, students seem disengaged and were obviously sleeping in class - the only thing that really matters, is doing well on the standardised tests.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: How polite and sociable everyone were. I expected the Koreans to be more introverted and keeping to themselves, but I honestly think most Danes would seem a lot more hostile and introverted to a foreigner

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) If you want to join a club, have some ideas in mind already before going, and ask specifically about clubs relating to those interests. 
2) Remember to take pictures!
3) Stay somewhere outside of Anam - otherwise you'll end up staying in the same area 24/7.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Talk to your professors in person! Navigating a foreign university-system can be hard and stressful; if you are stressed or struggling, talk to your professors about it, and they will certainly be ready to help guide you. I felt too intimidated to ask questions or ask for help in the beginning, but when I started talking to my professors about my struggles and worries, thay were actually very understanding and accomodating.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Learning to appreciate the things that I take for granted at home!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Being away from friends and family and the lack of freedom.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
